name: avatars
documentation: Deterministic initials avatars as SVG — a pure function of a name, with no network, no database, no image library and no font file — plus a guarded fetch for an avatar URL somebody supplied. The same name always gets the same colour, and the text colour is chosen by WCAG contrast rather than fixed, so a palette edit cannot leave unreadable initials behind.
//http-client-is-optional: Generating initials needs nothing, so declaring http.client as a requirement would make every route that wants an initials avatar load an HTTP client it never calls. The fetcher is bound only when HttpClientPort is already resolvable; a route that wants remoteImage() declares "requires": ["avatar.generation", "http.client"], and calling it without that throws with a message naming exactly that line.
//no-routes-the-fetch-would-be-an-open-p: Appwrite exposes this as GET /avatars/image?url=… — an unauthenticated endpoint that fetches an arbitrary URL and returns the bytes. That is an open proxy: anyone can use the server to reach what it can reach and they cannot — a metadata service, an internal admin panel — and read the answer out of the response. It is also a free bandwidth amplifier. So the capability is a service method and the application decides who may call it.
//the-url-came-from-a-user: Every outbound default is overridden. block_private => true, because the client allows private ranges by default for first-party gateways and that default lets a user point an avatar at http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and read IAM credentials out of the response. Redirects are not followed, which matters more here than anywhere: a 302 would let a remote host bounce the request to an internal address AFTER the guard approved the public one. A lowered max_response_bytes, because a hostile host could otherwise stream filler until the process ran out of memory. And retry => 0.
//the-content-type-is-read-from-the-byte: Never from the remote header. A host that declares image/png and sends HTML with a script in it would otherwise have those bytes re-served from our origin as image/png, and a browser without nosniff would sniff the real type and run it. SVG is refused outright and will not be supported: it is a scriptable document, so re-serving a stranger's SVG from your origin is stored XSS with no exploit required — and it is not detectable by magic bytes, because XML can begin with a declaration, a comment, a DOCTYPE, a BOM or whitespace.
//svg-out-is-different-from-svg-in: This plugin GENERATES SVG for initials and REFUSES SVG from third parties. Those are not in tension: one is a document whose entire text this code chose, the other is a file a stranger uploaded. The generated document is still served with a locked-down CSP and nosniff, and toDataUri() is offered because a browser will not run script in an SVG loaded through at all.
//no-icon-sets-no-qr-no-favicon-no-png: No browser, credit-card or country-flag icon sets: several hundred binary assets with a licence each, carried by every install, when a project can use any icon set — including flag emoji, which need no files. No QR codes: a correct encoder is Reed-Solomon over GF(256) and hundreds of lines that cannot be verified without known-answer vectors, and a wrapper around a library this plugin does not depend on would be untested glue. No favicon fetch: the same open-proxy problem, and the reliable version needs the site's HTML parsed for <link rel=icon>, so /favicon.ico alone would mostly not work. No PNG: rasterising needs GD or Imagick AND an embedded font with its licence; the cost is that many email clients do not render SVG, which the README states rather than solving badly.
